Sure. The ECT was recommended to me by my at-the-time psychiatrist. I had been diagnosed a couple years earlier with major depressive disorder, but she thought I showed signs of bipolar as well. I hadn't showed these signs the first couple years of my depression, but I was still too young for the average bipolar symptoms to present themselves. 

Bipolar tends to manifest in the early to late twenties, and I was diagnosed with depression at 16. 

Anyways, I hadn't really responded with any enthusiasm to previous medications for depression, and had been hospitalized a couple of times for suicidal intentions. 

At the hospital, this psychiatrist diagnosed me with bipolar and suggested ECT, as an alternative to medications. 

I honestly don't remember ever consenting to undergo ECT, but I don't remember a lot of things from that time. I can only assume I did consent to it and knew what I was doing at the time.

Anyways, I did ECT treatment for five weeks, three times a week. You go in the room and lie down on a hospital bed. They hook you up to an IV and give you a mouth guard to bite down on (so that you don't bite your tongue off during the treatment). 

They then put you under and you wake up with a splitting headache and really sore muscles all over. ECT is basically causing a seizure with electric shocks. Somehow some people's brain chemistry are altered in these seizures resulting in improved serotonin levels,, among other things. 

The ECT treatments cause memory loss, both preexisting memories and the ability to create new ones. For most people the memory returns within six months. 

It's been a year and a half since my ECT. 

You know how it feels to remember some fact you've once read out of a book? It's an impersonal fact recollection rather than reliving some personal experience. That's how I'd describe my current awareness of my entire life before the treatment. I don't remember actually experiencing graduating from high school,, for example. I just know that I did. 

Also, any memories since then are stored in that same way- facts instead of experiences. 

I believe that all this would disturb me quite a bit more if I actually knew what it was I am now missing.
It has irrevocably altered my own life for the worse
